title: Jev integration
seoTitle: Jev AI Integration for Business Workflows | EFIops
metaDescription: Integrate TypeSafe's Jev into applications for intent routing and structured decisions. Define workflows, evaluate uncertain cases and keep action rules in your code.
h1: Turn a request into the right next step.
lead: A question, an action and an unclear request need different responses. Use TypeSafe’s Jev to help choose a defined route, then let your application check access, apply the rules and handle what comes next.

sections.heading: Give each part of the system a clear job.
paragraphs: Jev is designed to return structured decisions from a supplied state and typed questions. In an assistant, a conversational model can handle dialogue while Jev helps identify a route. The application then checks permissions, retrieves the relevant information and decides which workflow may run.

sections.heading: Where a Jev integration may fit.
items: Intent classification. Distinguish a request for information from a request for action or human help.
Workflow routing. Map a supported intent to a defined next step.
Candidate evaluation. Explore scoring or selection against explicit criteria, with business rules applied separately.
Review handling. Use uncertainty signals alongside validation and permission checks to decide when a person should look.
Application integration. Connect the decision layer to an existing interface, API and monitoring view.

sections.heading: One request. A defined route.
paragraphs: A team member asks where to find material for a job. The system identifies the request, checks the user's access and runs an approved lookup. It presents the retrieved information or sends the unresolved request to a person.

sections.heading: A pilot built around your own examples.
paragraphs: We define the supported routes, assemble representative requests and test both clear and ambiguous cases. The pilot records what route was chosen, whether the result was useful and when human review was needed.
Thresholds are selected from evaluation results and the consequences of a mistake. A confidence value does not replace access control or establish that a decision is correct.

faqs.question: Do we need to replace our conversational AI?
faqs.answer: Not necessarily. A structured decision layer can be evaluated alongside an existing conversational interface.

faqs.question: Can Jev directly authorise an action?
faqs.answer: Authorisation belongs in your application. A model output may suggest a route; the software must still check whether the user and workflow are allowed to take it.

faqs.question: What happens when a request is ambiguous?
faqs.answer: The application can ask for clarification, collect more context or hand the request to a person.

faqs.question: Are you an official TypeSafe partner?
faqs.answer: EFIops is an independent integration provider. No official partnership or endorsement is claimed.

cta.label: Discuss a Jev integration
cta.heading: What decision would your software benefit from making?
cta.text: Bring a few real examples and the possible outcomes. We can evaluate whether Jev is a useful fit.

primaryIntent: Jev integration; TypeSafe AI developer; structured AI workflow decisions.
summary: Route requests into defined outcomes, with permission and action rules kept in your application.

useCases.title: A lookup or a stock movement?
useCases.body: Distinguish a question about availability from an action that changes a record. Apply a separate permission check before any change.

useCases.title: Who needs to deal with this?
useCases.body: Map a supported request to a team or workflow, and ask for clarification when essential context is missing.

useCases.title: Which option fits the criteria?
useCases.body: Evaluate candidates against explicit requirements, then test the routes against ordinary and difficult cases before expanding the pilot.

journey.heading: From a natural-language request to a defined application route.
journey.example: An operational application needs to separate stock questions from stock changes.
journey.question: A lookup, an action or a question to clarify?
journey.boundary: A route never replaces the application’s permission and action checks.

stages.label: Understand
stages.title: Map the requests and the existing application.
stages.body: We inspect the workflows, available context and application rules. A question about an item and a request to move it may sound similar, but they need different routes and different permissions.
stages.output: A request catalogue and an application-boundary map.

stages.label: Agree
stages.title: Define the routes before connecting the model.
stages.body: We agree the supported request types, expected structured outputs and what happens when details are missing. Access checks and state changes remain in application code, with the exact integration reviewed against Jev’s current interface.
stages.output: A route contract, integration scope and validation rules.

stages.label: Build
stages.title: Build the connection inside the workflow.
stages.body: A reviewable slice turns a request into a defined route and passes the validated result to the application. You can inspect the context, route and next action while the integration is being developed.
stages.output: A reviewable integration with explicit application handling.

stages.label: Test
stages.title: Try ambiguous, unsupported and action requests.
stages.body: We test representative requests against the expected routes. Malformed outputs, missing identifiers and disallowed actions need a visible fallback rather than a guessed or unchecked operation.
stages.output: Routing checks, output validation and fallback behaviour.

stages.label: Hand over
stages.title: Document the contract and its dependencies.
stages.body: The handover explains routes, context, provider configuration and the application checks around each action. Changes to the route set or model integration need review and regression checks.
stages.output: A route guide, dependency inventory and maintenance plan.

tests.label: Stock question
tests.reason: The application checks access before retrieving location.

tests.label: Stock change
tests.reason: The application validates permissions before any state change.

tests.label: Missing details
tests.reason: Ask which item and when it is needed.

handover.title: Route contract
handover.body: Supported requests, required fields and the application handler for each route.

handover.title: Application checks
handover.body: Where permissions, validation and approval are enforced around actions.

handover.title: Dependencies & review
handover.body: Integration configuration, supported interfaces and checks after a route or provider change.
